blocks.h2: Does Your Arlington Heights Home Need an Overhead Sewer?

tiles.h3: Your Home Was Built Before About 1980
tiles.body: Newer homes in Arlington Heights have been built with overhead sewers since the late 1970s or early 1980s. Older ones usually weren't.

tiles.h3: The Floor Drain Rises in Heavy Rain
tiles.body: Water comes up during a storm and goes back down after. That's the sewer pushing back.

tiles.h3: Your Line Is Clear and It Still Happens
tiles.body: No roots, no crack, and it still backs up. The problem is the sewer, not your pipe.

tiles.h3: You Want to Finish the Basement
tiles.body: Protecting it before the new floors go in costs less than replacing them later.

blocks.h2: How an Overhead Sewer System Works
blocks.body: Your upstairs fixtures drain out above the point where the sewer could back up into them. An overhead system gives the basement the same protection. Basement fixtures and the floor drain are rerouted to a sealed pit. An [ejector pump](/arlington-heights/ejector-pump) lifts that water to a pipe near the basement ceiling, and a check valve stops it from falling back. From there, gravity takes it to the sewer. The old floor drain connection is plugged, so the sewer has no low opening to push through.

blocks.h2: Why Overhead Sewers Make Sense in Arlington Heights
blocks.intro: The village has required overhead sewers in new construction since the late 1970s or early 1980s. That leaves many older homes with gravity drains in the basement.

items.body: Almost 7 inches of rain fell in just over three hours. Afterward, village officials pointed to overhead sewers as the main way to stop sewage backups.
Parts of older Arlington Heights, mainly near the center of town, have combined sewers. In heavy rain they fill with storm water, and a gravity floor drain is the first place it shows up.

items.h3: Fix the Line First If That's the Problem
items.body: We camera your line before recommending a conversion. If roots or a break are the real cause, a [sewer repair](/arlington-heights/sewer-repair) may be all you need.

blocks.h2: Overhead Sewer Questions From Arlington Heights Homeowners

items.q: How do I know if my home already has an overhead sewer?
items.preview: Look for a sealed pit with a pump and a pipe running up near the ceiling.
items.answer: Look for a sealed basin in the basement floor with a pump and a pipe running up the wall toward the ceiling. If your floor drain connects straight down into the floor, you likely have gravity drains. We can confirm in one visit.

items.q: Will an overhead sewer stop all basement water?
items.preview: It stops sewer backups. Groundwater needs a sump pump.
items.answer: It stops sewer water from coming up through basement drains. Groundwater seeping through walls or the floor is a [sump pump](/arlington-heights/sump-pumps) job. Many homes need both.

items.q: I have a basement bathroom. Can it stay?
items.preview: Yes. It drains to the ejector pit like the rest of the basement.
items.answer: Yes. A basement bathroom, laundry and bar sink all drain to the new pit, and the pump sends everything up and out. We'll size the pump for what you have.

items.q: How long does an overhead sewer installation take?
items.preview: Usually a few days, depending on the basement.
items.answer: Usually a few days, depending on how many fixtures there are and how finished the basement is. You'll get a schedule before we start.

items.q: How much does an overhead sewer system cost in Arlington Heights?
items.preview: It depends on your basement and the line. You get a flat price first.
items.answer: It depends on the depth of the sewer, the basement layout, how many fixtures are being rerouted and access. We give you a flat-rate price before any work begins.
